questions.text:
Node X has a TCP connection open to node Y. The packets from X to Y go through an intermediate IP router R. Ethernet switch S is the first switch on the network path between X and R. Consider a packet sent from X to Y over this connection.
Which of the following statements is/are TRUE about the destination IP and MAC addresses on this packet at the time it leaves X?
questions.solution:
Recall how addresses change along the path:
- IP addresses are end-to-end: the destination IP stays the IP of Y on the whole path.
- MAC addresses are hop-by-hop: the destination MAC is that of the next IP hop, which is router R. A switch only forwards frames; it is never the destination MAC.

So the only true statement is: destination IP = IP of Y.

Answer: The destination IP address is the IP address of Y

Click here for detail solution by gateoverflow
options: The destination IP address is the IP address of R
The destination IP address is the IP address of Y
The destination MAC address is the MAC address of S
The destination MAC address is the MAC address of Y

questions.text: Consider sending an IP datagram of size 1420 bytes (including 20 bytes of IP header) from a sender to a receiver over a path of two links with a router between them. The first link (sender to router) has an MTU (Maximum Transmission Unit) size of 542 bytes, while the second link (router to receiver) has an MTU size of 360 bytes. The number of fragments that would be delivered at the receiver is _____
questions.solution:
Data in datagram [latex]=1420-20=1400[/latex] bytes. Fragment data (except the last) must be a multiple of 8.

Link 1 (MTU 542): max data [latex]=522[/latex] [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] use 520. Fragments: 520, 520, 360.
Link 2 (MTU 360): max data [latex]=340[/latex] [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] use 336.
- 520 [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] 336 + 184
- 520 [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] 336 + 184
- 360 [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] 336 + 24

Fragments are reassembled only at the receiver, so it receives [latex]2+2+2=6[/latex] fragments.

Answer: 6

questions.text:
Consider the entries shown below in the forwarding table of an [latex] \mathbb{P} [/latex] router. Each entry consists of an IP prefix and the corresponding next hop router for packets whose destination IP address matches the prefix. The notation "[latex] \mathrm{/N} [/latex]" in a prefix indicates a subnet mask with the most significant [latex] \mathrm{N} [/latex] bits set to 1.

[latex] \begin{array}{|l|c|} \hline Prefix & Next\; hop \; router \\ \hline 10.1 .1 .0 / 24 & R1 \\ \hline 10.1 .1 .128 / 25 & R2 \\ \hline 10.1 .1 .64 / 26 & R3 \\ \hline 10.1 .1 .192 / 26 & R4 \\ \hline \end{array}[/latex]

This router forwards 20 packets each to 5 hosts. The IP addresses of the hosts are 10.1.1.16, 10.1.1.72, 10.1.1.132, 10.1.1.191, and 10.1.1.205. The number of packets forwarded via the next hop router [latex] R 2 [/latex] is
questions.solution:
Use longest prefix match. Address ranges (last byte):
/24 [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] 0-255 (R1), .128/25 [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] 128-255 (R2), .64/26 [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] 64-127 (R3), .192/26 [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] 192-255 (R4).

- 10.1.1.16 [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] only /24 [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] R1
- 10.1.1.72 [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] /26 (64-127) [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] R3
- 10.1.1.132 [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] /25 [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] R2
- 10.1.1.191 [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] /25 (not in 192-255) [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] R2
- 10.1.1.205 [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] /26 (192-255) [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] R4

R2 gets 2 hosts [latex]\times[/latex] 20 packets [latex]=40[/latex].

Answer: 40

questions.text:
Consider a network path [latex]\mathrm{P}-\mathrm{Q}-\mathrm{R} [/latex] between nodes [latex]\mathrm{P} [/latex] and [latex]\mathrm{R} [/latex] via router [latex]\mathrm{Q} [/latex]. Node [latex]\mathrm{P} [/latex] sends a file of size [latex]10^6 [/latex] bytes to [latex]R [/latex] via this path by splitting the file into chunks of [latex]10^3 [/latex] bytes each. Node [latex]P [/latex] sends these chunks one after the other without any wait time between the successive chunk transmissions. Assume that the size of extra headers added to these chunks is negligible, and that the chunk size is less than the MTU.
Each of the links [latex]\mathrm{P}-\mathrm{Q} [/latex] and [latex]\mathrm{Q}-\mathrm{R} [/latex] has a bandwidth of [latex]10^6 \mathrm{bits} / \mathrm{sec} [/latex], and negligible propagation latency. Router [latex]Q [/latex] immediately transmits every packet it receives from [latex]P [/latex] to [latex]R [/latex], with negligible processing and queueing delays. Router [latex]Q [/latex] can simultaneously receive on link [latex]P-Q [/latex] and transmit on [latex]\operatorname{link} Q-R [/latex].
Assume P starts transmitting the chunks at time [latex]t=0 [/latex]. Which one of the following options gives the time (in seconds, rounded off to 3 decimal places) at which [latex]\mathrm{R} [/latex] receives all the chunks of the file?
questions.solution:
Number of chunks [latex]=10^6/10^3=1000[/latex]. Each chunk [latex]=8000[/latex] bits, so transmission time on a link [latex]=\frac{8000}{10^6}=8[/latex] ms.

P sends the chunks back to back: the last chunk is fully sent by P at [latex]1000\times8\text{ ms}=8[/latex] s.
Q forwards each chunk while receiving the next, so only the last chunk adds one more transmission of 8 ms on Q-R.

Total [latex]=8+0.008=8.008[/latex] s.

Answer: 8.008

Click here for detail solution by gateoverflow

questions.text:
Which of the following fields is/are modified in the IP header of a packet going out
of a network address translation (NAT) device from an internal network to an
external network?
questions.solution:
For an outgoing packet, NAT replaces the private source IP (and port) with its public IP.

Because a header field changed, the header checksum must be recomputed.

Destination IP is unchanged (it is the outside server), and total length is unchanged (payload size is the same).

Answer: Source IP, Header Checksum
